source: Goodman, Mansinghka, Roy, Bonawitz, Tenenbaum (2008) Church: a language for generative models
finding: Church defines a stochastic lambda calculus. Inference is conditioning by query, implemented with rejection sampling and Metropolis-Hastings over the program's random choices.
numbers: Systems and expressiveness paper. No human-subject data. Inference shown on small examples only.
limits: Boundary: the generic samplers are slow on hard conditioning (rejection fails for low-probability evidence).
agent_relevance: A thinking schema can treat condition-and-query as a primitive, but needs an efficient inference step, not naive rejection.

source: Goodman et al. (2008) Church (inference section)
finding: A collapsed rejection sampler wastes work, so the paper builds an MH chain over computation traces. Chain initialization itself hits the rejection problem.
numbers: No speed numbers in the text read. Qualitative statement of the initialization problem.
limits: Later systems (WebPPL, Gen, SMC steering) exist mostly to fix this cost.
agent_relevance: Naive generate-and-test is the weak baseline. Reuse partial work (resample, do not restart).

source: Wong, Grand, Lew, Goodman, Mansinghka, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2023) From word models to world models: rational meaning construction
finding: Proposes LLM translation from language to Church code (probabilistic language of thought) plus Bayesian inference. Examples: tug-of-war, kinship, scenes, agents.
numbers: No quantitative human or benchmark evaluation. The authors call the examples illustrative and pedagogical. Zero effect sizes.
limits: Proof of concept only. Success claims rest on chosen examples. Later papers supply numbers.
agent_relevance: Useful pattern: LLM writes the model, a solver does the reasoning. Do not cite it as evidence of accuracy.

source: Wong et al. (2023) From word models to world models (versus step-by-step LLM reasoning)
finding: Argues chain-of-thought can be unfaithful, and that Prolog-style tool use handles only deduction. Probabilistic programs add defeasible updating.
numbers: Argument with citations (Golovneva 2022, Lyu 2023 and others). No new measurement.
limits: ProbLog is named as an equally valid target language, so Church is not special.
agent_relevance: Language choice (Church, ProbLog, Python PPL) is open. Test it, do not assume.

source: Ying, Zhi-Xuan, Wong, Mansinghka, Tenenbaum (2024) Grounding language about belief in a Bayesian theory of mind
finding: A Bayesian theory-of-mind model (probabilistic program plus epistemic logic) predicts human belief ratings far better than non-mentalizing baselines.
numbers: N=100 Prolific participants, 9 of 18 scenarios each. Belief-statement r: full BToM 0.92 [0.91,0.93]; heuristic mentalizer 0.86 and 0.04 (two priors); non-mentalizer 0.19; omniscient observer 0.19; ignorant observer 0.64. Goal attribution r=0.93 [0.91,0.94].
limits: One gridworld (doors, keys, gems). Hand-built model. Heuristic mentalizer with the wrong prior collapses to r=0.04, so fit depends on modeling choices.
agent_relevance: A structured model beats shortcuts by a large margin, but only when the generative model is right. Prior choice is a fragile point.

source: Ying et al. (2024) Grounding language about belief (prior sensitivity)
finding: Same model with a uniform-over-states belief prior instead of uniform-over-statements drops from r=0.92 to r=0.86.
limits: Moderate sensitivity here; a different prior in the heuristic mentalizer gave 0.04.
agent_relevance: Report sensitivity to priors as a routine check on any model the agent writes.

source: Grand, Pepe, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2024) Loose LIPS sink ships: Battleship with language-informed program sampling
finding: LLM proposes questions, translates them to programs, scores expected information gain (EIG). A small sample budget reaches human-level questions.
numbers: Human data N=40, 605 question-board pairs. Single-sample EIG: CodeLlama 0.65, GPT-4 0.66, grammar 0.36. k=5 samples: both LLMs near human mean; k=10 beat human mean (p<0.001 CodeLlama, p=0.01 GPT-4). 40% (CodeLlama) and 33% (GPT-4) of sampled programs had EIG=0.
limits: Still below the best human questions at all k. Needs an existing DSL. Translation success 75% (CodeLlama), 88% (GPT-4).
agent_relevance: Sample-and-score beat one-shot generation: 5 to 10 samples with a scoring rule lifted quality above single draws.

source: Grand et al. (2024) Loose LIPS (GPT-4V grounding)
finding: GPT-4V given the board image did no better than with no board at all.
numbers: Textual board format was the only one that beat no-board (p<0.05 for k=1-20). Visual format was significantly worse (k=1,5) or equal (k=10-50).
limits: 2024 snapshots (gpt-4-0613, gpt-4-vision-preview). May be outdated.
agent_relevance: Pure LLMs can fail at grounding even with the evidence in context. External scoring against the real state fixes it.

source: Ying, Collins, Wei, Zhang, Zhi-Xuan, Weller, Tenenbaum, Wong (2023) NIPE: neuro-symbolic inverse planning engine
finding: LLM translates language to a symbolic goal-inference problem, then inverse planning computes the posterior. It tracks human judgments much better than GPT-4 or GPT-3.5 asked directly.
limits: GPT-4 near zero on the Colored-Different variant (ignored a stated key rule) and weaker on Spatial. GPT-3.5 negative on one variant. March 2023 models. Small N.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM answers drop on rules that change world dynamics. A solver that executes the rule is robust to this.

source: Collins, Wong, Feng, Wei, Tenenbaum (2022) Structured, flexible, and robust: benchmarking LLMs on out-of-distribution reasoning
finding: GPT-3 text was rated lower than human text in planning and explanation, and the two differed in how they reacted to added constraints. A hybrid language-to-program model was proposed.
numbers: Blind raters N=393 (7-point scale) plus N=370 for language-error screening. Humans beat the LLM in every condition (p<0.001, likelihood ratio test). Significant source-by-condition interaction.
limits: Only GPT-3 tested. Rater preference is a proxy for reasoning quality. The hybrid model is a small proof of concept.
agent_relevance: Out-of-distribution constraints are where a model-based scaffold has most to gain.

source: Ellis (2023) Human-like few-shot learning via Bayesian reasoning over natural language
finding: Hypotheses are proposed in natural language by an LLM and reweighted by Bayes. A fitted prior and about 50-100 proposals fit human concept learning.
numbers: Number Game: average of 8 human participants; 50-100 samples needed, versus over 5000 hypotheses in the classic model. Logical concepts: R2=0.81 with 100 proposals per batch, within 3% of human accuracy and above GPT-4 alone.
limits: Prior tuning was critical for logical concepts. Human data are small and averaged across groups. GPT-4 alone differed from humans, though no ground truth exists for the Number Game.
agent_relevance: Verbalised hypothesis plus Bayes update is a cheap, interpretable alternative to long chains of thought. The prior needs tuning.

source: Piriyakulkij, Langenfeld, Le, Ellis (2024) Doing experiments and revising rules with natural language and probabilistic reasoning
finding: Online SMC over natural-language rules explains Zendo human data better than batch inference or a direct LLM agent. Fuzzy rules fit people better than hard rules, although hard rules score higher accuracy.
numbers: Human accuracy 5.26/8 (data from Bramley et al.); ReAct-style direct LLM 4.60/8; best model 6.55/8. Fit to human accuracy by rule: online fuzzy R2=0.57; hard rules R2=0.10; batch inference R2=0.05; direct LLM R2=0.25. Per-scene fit of online fuzzy R2=0.35.
limits: LLMs revise hypotheses well but do not consistently beat random guessing when proposing experiments. Narrow task family (Zendo and a few others).
agent_relevance: Revising a small pool of hypotheses online beat batch refinement. LLM experiment proposals were weak, so they need a scoring step.

source: Tsividis, Loula, Burga, Foss, Campero, Pouncy, Gershman, Tenenbaum (2021) Human-level RL through theory-based modeling, exploration, and planning
finding: EMPA (programs for a game engine, Bayesian model learning, planning) matches human learning curves on 90 novel games. Double DQN and Rainbow make little or no progress at human timescales.
numbers: 90 games. Humans learn in minutes (a few hundred steps). Baselines DDQN and Rainbow. Exact per-game scores not extracted.
limits: EMPA gets a symbolic object-level input and a hand-built hypothesis space. Not end-to-end from pixels.
agent_relevance: Strong structure in the hypothesis space gives big sample efficiency. For the agent, structure must be supplied or synthesised.

source: Wong et al. (2025) Modeling open-world cognition as on-demand synthesis of probabilistic models
finding: A Model Synthesis Architecture (LLM-written WebPPL models built on demand) matches human judgments better than LLM-only baselines, most of all when novel variables are introduced.
numbers: Three human experiments (sports vignettes: tug-of-war, canoe, biathlon). Base model Llama-3.1-70B; 1000 samples (Exp 1-2), 500 (Exp 3). MSA fits fell within the human split-half 95% CI. Exp 3 (open-world) showed the largest gap to LM-only. Exact R2 values are in figures and were not extracted.
limits: Exp 1 replicates the 2014 tug-of-war result; no hand-built baseline exists for Exp 3. MSA variance too low in places; models miss fine distribution structure of human judgments. One domain was dropped for very low inter-participant correlation.
agent_relevance: On-demand model writing helps most under distribution shift. Warning: agreement with human means can hide wrong variance.

source: Wong et al. (2025) Modeling open-world cognition (coherence explanation)
finding: Authors suggest LM baselines miss human judgments partly because their implied beliefs are not coherent; synthesised models are coherent by design.
numbers: Interpretive claim. No separate coherence test reported in the text read.
limits: Untested explanation. A competing one: the LM baselines were prompted one way only.
agent_relevance: Test coherence directly (do answers to related queries obey probability rules?) before assuming a solver is needed.

source: Lew, Zhi-Xuan, Grand, Mansinghka (2023) Sequential Monte Carlo steering of LLMs using probabilistic programs
finding: Frames constrained generation as posterior inference in a language-model probabilistic program, solved by SMC. Argues beam search over-values short high-probability completions.
numbers: Workshop abstract. Example: a two-token completion has log probability -11.74 under LLaMA-7b yet beats any single long completion.
limits: No benchmark numbers in the abstract. A quantitative comparison appears only in later work.
agent_relevance: Argument for sampling over single-path decoding when constraints exist.

source: Loula et al. (2025) Syntactic and semantic control of LLMs via sequential Monte Carlo
finding: SMC with cheap and expensive checks beats locally constrained decoding, sample-rerank, and importance sampling across four tasks.
numbers: Table 2 (small Llama models): goal inference base 0.063, full SMC 0.419; molecular synthesis base 0.132, full SMC 0.577; text-to-SQL base 0.531, full SMC 0.620. Data science base 0.213, best 0.407. Full SMC beat full importance sampling with one-tenth of the particles in 3 of 4 domains, one-fifth in the fourth.
limits: Tasks use formal checkers. Gains need a verifiable potential. Small base models.
agent_relevance: Spend effort on verifiers and resampling during generation, not only at the end.

source: Loula et al. (2025) SMC control: ablations
finding: Expensive semantic checks add most of the gain; weight corrections add smaller gains and sometimes none.
numbers: Expensive potential: large gain in goal inference, data science, molecules; smaller but significant (permutation p<0.01) in text-to-SQL. Weight correction had no effect on goal inference and molecules when the expensive check was present.
limits: Ablations on 1B-8B models; larger models may shrink the gap.
agent_relevance: Invest in verifier checks, not fancy inference corrections.

source: Loula et al. (2025) SMC control versus SMC steering
finding: Newer SMC method versus the 2023 steering method on text-to-SQL is nearly tied.
numbers: Full SMC (10 particles) 0.620 (0.60,0.64) vs SMC Steering (5 particles) 0.607 (0.58,0.63). Intervals overlap.
limits: Different particle counts; not a clean contest.
agent_relevance: Do not expect large wins from inference-algorithm refinements once a good checker exists.

source: Lake, Salakhutdinov, Tenenbaum (2015) Human-level concept learning through probabilistic program induction
finding: Bayesian program learning matched or beat humans at one-shot character classification and passed a visual Turing test for generated characters.
numbers: Recalled, unverified: one-shot error about 3.3% (BPL) vs 4.5% humans vs about 8% deep networks; judges barely above chance at spotting machine drawings.
limits: Not opened this session (search budget exhausted, publisher pages blocked); recorded from prior knowledge, verify before citing.
agent_relevance: A generative program model can beat large networks with one example, in a narrow domain.

source: Jones and Love (2011) Bayesian fundamentalism or enlightenment? On the explanatory status of Bayesian models of cognition
finding: Critique: Bayesian cognitive models often fit data with flexible priors and likelihoods and ignore mechanism and constraints.
numbers: No numbers. Argument paper with commentaries.
limits: Not opened this session (search budget exhausted, publisher pages blocked); recorded from prior knowledge, verify before citing.
agent_relevance: Fit alone does not discriminate theories. Ask for out-of-sample tests.

source: Bowers and Davis (2012) Bayesian just-so stories in psychology and neuroscience
finding: Critique: Bayesian accounts can be post hoc, with priors and utilities tuned to the data, and sometimes lose to simpler non-Bayesian accounts.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened this session (search budget exhausted, publisher pages blocked); recorded from prior knowledge, verify before citing.
agent_relevance: Fix the model and priors before looking at the data when the agent evaluates its own models.

source: Marcus and Davis (2013) How robust are probabilistic models of higher-level cognition?
finding: Critique: re-analyses of several probabilistic-model studies suggest fits depend on selective choice of task, data and model.
numbers: Recalled, unverified: reasonable alternative choices weakened the fits.
limits: Not opened this session (search budget exhausted, publisher pages blocked); recorded from prior knowledge, verify before citing.
agent_relevance: Same caution as the BToM prior-sensitivity lines: model choice and prior tuning drive fit.

source: Wong et al. (2025) Exp 1 as replication of the 2014 tug-of-war finding
finding: The authors describe Exp 1 as essentially replicating the earlier tug-of-war probabilistic-model finding, now with synthesised models.
numbers: Exp 1 used detailed background text; MSA fits within human split-half range. Original 2014 numbers not read.
limits: Same research group and stimulus family. No independent lab replication found this session.
agent_relevance: Independent replication is thin in this subfield. Treat claims as single-lab.

source: Wong et al. (2025) human-human agreement as a ceiling
finding: Model-human agreement is judged against a human split-half baseline. One domain was dropped when humans disagreed with each other.
numbers: Fits generally fall within the 95% CI of human-human split-half. MSA distributions about as close to humans as humans are to each other (Wasserstein and TVD).
limits: Split-half reliability limits what a model can show. Non-expert judgments on novel stimuli are noisy.
agent_relevance: Check for a human noise ceiling before calling a gap a failure.

source: Ying et al. (2024) BToM: what makes it hold
finding: Removing the link from goals to instrumental plans hurts the fit, so the gain comes from joint inference of goals, beliefs and plans.
numbers: Heuristic mentalizer (no instrumental plans) r=0.86 or 0.04 vs full 0.92; non-mentalizer 0.19; omniscient 0.19.
limits: Single task; humans watched short gridworld clips.
agent_relevance: What matters is whether the structure captures what the observer can know.
